notes: The opening phrase, There once was a man, can introduce either a parable (2 Sam 12:1) or history (1 Sam 25:2). • Job is also mentioned in Ezekiel 14:14, Ezekiel 14:20 and James 5:11. • Uz is east of the Jordan, either in Edom to the south (Genesis 36:28; 1 Chr 1:42; Jeremiah 25:19-20; Lamentations 4:21) or in Aram to the north (Genesis 10:23; Genesis 22:21; 1 Chr 1:17, 42). Job was not an Israelite—he lived before the nation was born and outside its later territory. • Job was morally blameless—a man of complete integrity (Job 1:8; Job 2:3; see Psalm 25:21; Psalm 37:37; Proverbs 2:7; Proverbs 20:11; Proverbs 29:10). He did not claim to be perfect or sinless (Job 6:24; Job 7:21; see also Ecclesiastes 7:20; Romans 3:23; 1 Jn 1:8), but he was righteous; his suffering did not result from guilt. He feared God (see Psalm 111:10; Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10; 2 Cor 7:1) and did not appeal to any of the ancient Near Eastern gods (Job 9:8; Job 23:13; Job 31:26-28).
God and Satan agree to a test that would bring about Job’s troubles and confirm his integrity (Job 1:20-21; Job 2:10). None of the book’s characters ever learn of this heavenly council.

Job was prosperous in sons, daughters, livestock, and servants (cp. Genesis 30:43; Deuteronomy 7:13; Psalm 107:38). • Numbers such as seven and three (and 7,000 and 3,000) indicate the completeness of the blessing Job experienced (see Job 42:13; see also Psalm 127:3-5; Psalm 128:3). • the richest person in that entire area: The figures that catalogue Job’s wealth might not be exact, but they are realistic for a wealthy man of that time (cp. Nabal’s wealth, 1 Sam 25:2).

Ritual washing and changing garments were common ways for individuals to purify themselves before offering a sacrifice (Genesis 35:2; Exodus 19:10, Exodus 19:14). • The common time for conscientious piety was early in the morning (see Genesis 22:3; Psalm 5:3; Mark 1:35). • cursed: The Hebrew term barak (literally blessed) is used here as a euphemism for cursing (cp. Job 1:11; Job 2:5, Job 2:9; 1 Kgs 21:10, 13; Psalm 10:3). Job was concerned that his children might have committed this capital crime (Leviticus 24:10-16; 1 Kgs 21:9-13; cp. Job 1:11; Job 2:5, Job 2:9). Job understood that sinful attitudes in people’s hearts constitute sin (Jeremiah 17:9-10; Mark 7:21-23).

The members of the heavenly court are heavenly beings; they may be either holy angels or rebellious demons (Genesis 6:2, Genesis 6:4). They join God in his deliberations, including at creation (Genesis 1:26) and in his rule over creation (Job 1:6; Genesis 3:22; Genesis 2:1; 1 Kgs 22:19-22; Psalm 82:1; Psalm 89:5, Psalm 89:7-8; Daniel 3:13, Daniel 3:17, Daniel 3:23, Daniel 3:25; Daniel 7:9-14). • The account remains unclear as to whether Satan usually came with other members of the heavenly court to make a report or whether he was intruding as Job’s adversary. • Where have you come from? The question was God’s sovereign demand for a report from a subordinate (see Genesis 3:9). • Satan was not patrolling to implement God’s judgments (cp. 1 Chr 21:1-14; 2 Kgs 19:35 // Isaiah 37:36; Ezekiel 1:5-9) but to oppose God’s purposes (2 Tim 2:26; 1 Pet 5:8).
my servant: This title was used for the patriarchs (Genesis 26:24; Exodus 32:13), the prophets (2 Kgs 17:13; Jeremiah 7:25; Zechariah 1:6), and David (e.g., 2 Sam 7:1-29; Psalm 18:1; Psalm 36:1).

Job has good reason (Hebrew khinnam; see study note on 2:3) to fear God: The wisdom tradition links piety with prosperity. Satan went a step further by suggesting that Job’s piety was contingent upon his affluence.
wall of protection: See 1 Sam 25:16; Psalm 5:12; Psalm 34:7; Zechariah 2:5; cp. Isaiah 5:5.

reach out . . . test him . . . Do whatever you want: Satan was God’s agent; the hand he put forth was the Lord’s as well as Satan’s, for here they acted against everything Job possessed and later against Job himself (Job 2:5-6). • Job later cursed the day of his birth (Job 3:1, Job 3:8), but he did not curse God (Job 31:30), even when his distraught wife urged him to do so (Job 2:9). • God allowed Satan to test Job to prove that Satan’s cynicism was incorrect (1 Cor 10:11; see James 1:13; cp. Luke 22:31-32; John 19:11).

These attacks destroyed the blessings enumerated in Job 1:2-3; Job was left alone with the four ominous messengers who came to report and a wife who offered misguided counsel. • The repetition of while he was still speaking emphasizes the relentlessness of the attacks (see Jeremiah 51:31). The repetition of I am the only one who escaped to tell you emphasizes the total obliteration of Job’s resources.

The Sabeans were marauding bandit tribes from the desert (cp. Judges 6:3). By the 700s BC, the southern Sabeans would become a national power that traded in gold, precious stones, perfume, and slaves (Psalm 72:10; Isaiah 43:3; Isaiah 45:14; Isaiah 60:6; Jeremiah 6:20).
The fire of God . . . from heaven (Job 20:26) might have been lightning (Leviticus 10:2; 1 Kgs 18:38; 2 Kgs 1:10-14), wildfire (Numbers 11:1-3), or volcanic activity (Genesis 19:24).
That the wind . . . hit the house on all sides suggests that Job and his children were settled farmers living in houses rather than nomads living in tents.

Job tore his robe and shaved his head; both were common Near East rituals that demonstrated grief. These actions sometimes substituted for self-mutilation as a physical response to shock, horror, or bad news (Job 2:12; Genesis 37:29, Genesis 37:34; Judges 11:35; Jeremiah 16:6; Ezekiel 7:18; Amos 8:10). • He fell to the ground, not to wail in despair, but to worship in hope (1 Pet 5:6).
This scene is an exact repetition of the scene presented in Job 1:6-8.
The phrase without cause (Hebrew khinnam) is a wordplay on Satan’s question in Job 1:9.
take away his health (literally strike his flesh and bones): Bones were thought to be the seat of health.
spare (literally guard/watch over): God ironically made Satan responsible for guarding Job’s life (cp. Job 10:13-14; Job 13:27; Job 33:11).
This term for terrible boils was used for any inflamed, running sores (Exodus 9:10; Leviticus 13:18-20; Deuteronomy 28:27, Deuteronomy 28:35).

Job might have scraped his skin to relieve itching; the Greek Old Testament says that it was “to scrape away the pus.” • The ashes might refer to a place where lepers were quarantined, but Job was probably demonstrating his grief and dismay (Job 30:19; Genesis 18:27; 2 Sam 13:19; Isaiah 58:5; Jonah 3:6).

Job’s wife first summarized the essence of Job’s temptation by echoing God’s words (Job 2:3); Job was trying to maintain his integrity. In her frustration and anguish, however, she then counseled Job to curse God and thus unknowingly fulfill Satan’s prediction (Job 1:11; Job 2:5).

Job’s acceptance of bad as well as good things from God’s hand demonstrates his righteousness and faith (cp. Job 1:21; 2 Sam 12:16-20; Luke 22:42). • By saying nothing wrong, Job controlled his tongue (Proverbs 13:3; Proverbs 21:23; see James 3:2).

It might have taken several months for Job’s friends (see study note on 6:14-27) to hear of his afflictions (see Job 7:3). • The text implies that Job’s friends were Edomites, a people who were famous for their wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 1:8). • Eliphaz the Temanite was probably a descendant of Esau’s grandson Teman (Genesis 36:10-11, Genesis 36:15); his land was located in Edom (Ezekiel 25:13; Amos 1:11-12). • The Bil- element in Bildad would remind Hebrew readers of names like Bilhan, a descendant of Esau (Genesis 36:27; 1 Chr 1:42). The -dad element would remind them of names like Bedad, father of the Edomite king Hadad (Genesis 36:35; 1 Chr 1:46). • Shuhite: No place named Shuah is known, but Abraham’s son Shuah was sent to “a land in the east” (Genesis 25:1, Genesis 25:6; 1 Chr 1:32). • The Greek Old Testament lists Zophar instead of Zepho as one of Esau’s grandsons (Genesis 36:11, Genesis 36:15; 1 Chr 1:36). A Naamathite might reside in a town named Naamah, but no such location is known. Two Old Testament women are named Naamah, but neither is a likely ancestor of Zophar (Genesis 4:22; 1 Kgs 14:21).

they scarcely recognized him: This expression indicates the extreme suffering Job had experienced (cp. Isaiah 52:14; Isaiah 53:3). • Job’s friends mourned by wailing loudly, just as they would have done for a dead man. • Throwing dust sometimes expressed anger or disdain (see 2 Sam 16:13; Acts 22:23), but here it signaled mourning (see Joshua 7:6; 1 Sam 4:12; Nehemiah 9:1; Lamentations 2:10).

Job’s friends sat on the ground to identify with Job’s suffering (see Job 2:8). • The standard period for mourning the death of a notable person or for acknowledging other disastrous news was seven days and nights (Genesis 50:10; 1 Sam 31:13; see also Ezekiel 3:14-15).

Job spoke and thus put at risk his refusal to sin with his mouth (Job 1:21; Job 2:10). • Job cursed the day of his birth in great detail. However, his words sound more like pitiful complaints. Job didn’t curse God as his creator, but he lamented the conditions of his existence.

Job’s outburst did not mean that his integrity had cracked under the strain (Job 42:7-8; James 5:11). Elijah and Jeremiah, both godly men, used the same hyperbolic language (1 Kgs 19:4; Jeremiah 20:14-18).
Job longed for the sinister darkness of the underworld (Exodus 10:22; Proverbs 4:19; Joel 2:2) and the gloom of death (Job 10:21-22; Job 38:17) to claim the day of his birth.
The expression experts at cursing refers to professional cursers such as Balaam (Numbers 22:1–24:25).
Venus and Mercury, the morning stars, herald the dawn (Job 38:7).

shut my mother’s womb: Closing or opening the womb sometimes refers to conception (Genesis 16:2; Genesis 20:18; Genesis 29:31; Genesis 30:22; 1 Sam 1:5-6), but here it refers to birth (see also Job 38:8).

Job’s language turns from curse to lamentation. Job alternates between repugnance for life and a romance with death. Seven times, Job laments his situation by asking why (Job 3:11, Job 3:12, Job 3:16, Job 3:20, Job 3:23; see Psalm 10:1; Psalm 22:1; Jeremiah 20:18; Lamentations 5:20).
The dead were thought to continue their identities and social status after death. Perhaps Job wanted the world’s kings and prime ministers to acknowledge his own princely status (Job 1:3).
rich in gold, whose palaces were filled with silver: This might refer to treasure-filled tombs, but it more likely refers to the futile hoarding of wealth that ends in death (as in Job 3:14).

Job equated light with life (Job 33:30; see John 1:4; John 8:12). • Bitter might mean “short-tempered” (Judges 18:25), “enraged” (2 Sam 17:8), “anguish” (Job 7:11), “distress” (Proverbs 31:6), or “discontented” (1 Sam 1:10; 22:2).
People in misery long for death with the desperation of those who dig for hidden treasure.

Eliphaz the Temanite (see study note on 2:11) was the most prominent and probably the oldest of Job’s friends; his speeches are longer and more ornate than the others. • who could keep from speaking out? Eliphaz mimicked the urgency of a prophetic revelation (Job 4:12-16; see Jeremiah 20:9; Amos 3:8).

This section begins three rounds of speeches by each of Job’s three comforters, each with a response from Job (Job 4:1–27:23). In this first round, Job’s friends exhort him to seek God so that he can again enjoy prosperity.
People . . . who were weak were depressed and suffered from low morale (Isaiah 13:7; Isaiah 35:3; Ezekiel 7:17).
Job probably counted his children among the innocent dead (Job 1:5), and even Eliphaz must have known that innocent blood is sometimes shed (cp. Deuteronomy 19:10; Proverbs 6:17; Jeremiah 7:6).

The harvest metaphor illustrates the scriptural principle that behavior merits judgment (Proverbs 22:8; Hosea 8:7; Romans 2:9-11; Galatians 6:7-8). The New Testament describes the final judgment as a harvest (Matthew 13:39). Jesus rejected simplistic attempts to analyze people’s lives by this principle (Luke 13:4; John 9:1-3).
They vanish in a blast of his anger: Eliphaz understood the wind of Job 1:19 as divine judgment (cp. Isaiah 40:7; Hosea 13:15).
Eliphaz posed as a prophet, implying that God spoke to him in secret (Numbers 12:6); later God did speak to him, but not to affirm his counsel (Job 42:7).
Eliphaz probably referred to the God-induced sleep associated with prophetic vision (Job 33:15; Genesis 15:12; Numbers 12:6; Isaiah 29:10).

Fear is common in God’s presence (Genesis 15:12; Daniel 8:17-18; Daniel 10:8-10), but God tells his people not to be afraid (Genesis 15:1; Genesis 26:24; Isaiah 40:9; Isaiah 44:8). • Eliphaz’s bones trembled like those of a prophet with terrible news to deliver (Jeremiah 23:9; Habakkuk 3:16).
A spirit (or wind) swept past my face: Wind is a physical display of God’s powerful presence (Job 38:1; Nahum 1:3; Acts 2:2; cp. 1 Kgs 19:11).

As the characters in the book repeatedly acknowledge, no one is truly innocent or pure (see Job 9:2; Job 15:14; Job 25:4; Job 35:7) because all are depraved (Psalm 14:3; Psalm 53:3; Romans 3:10-11). Eliphaz used these terms to mean that human beings are sinful creatures and God is the sinless Creator. Job and God used them to mean that Job had faithfully carried out the duties inherent in his relationship with God. Job and Eliphaz never agreed on the meaning of these terms. Later, God said that Eliphaz had spoken inaccurately (Job 42:7).
The concept that God does not trust his own angels and that he charged his messengers with foolishness is otherwise unknown (but see Genesis 6:1-4).
A tent was a common symbol for mortal life (Isaiah 38:12; 2 Cor 5:1; cp. Ecclesiastes 12:6).

The angels (literally the holy ones), probably a reference back to Job 4:18, are called “holy ones” because of their proximity to God, not because they were morally perfect (Job 15:15; Daniel 4:14; Daniel 8:13; Zechariah 14:5).
The court (literally the gate) was the site of legal and commercial deliberations in which Job had participated (Job 29:7; see Deuteronomy 21:19-21; Ruth 4:1-11).

To go to God meant lodging a formal appeal with God for assistance, counsel, or vindication, sometimes by way of repentance (Amos 5:4, Amos 5:6) and possibly through a prophetic oracle (Genesis 25:22; 1 Sam 9:9; 1 Kgs 22:8). • Job wanted to present his case to God (Job 13:3, Job 13:15, Job 13:18; Job 23:3-8), and later he attempted to do so (Job 29:1–31:40).
Job’s region depended upon rain rather than irrigation (see Job 36:27-28).
Eliphaz’s doxology praised God as the wonder-working Creator and Sustainer of the universe (Job 5:9-10) and as the righteous Judge who brings down the powerful and lifts up the poor (Job 5:11-16).
God traps the wise in the cleverness of their words (Proverbs 12:13). Paul alluded to this verse in his rejection of worldly wisdom (1 Cor 1:19).
the discipline of the Almighty: See Deuteronomy 8:5; Proverbs 3:11-12; Revelation 3:19.

six disasters . . . even in the seventh: This wisdom formula reflects a sense of completeness (cp. Proverbs 30:15-31). • This list reflects Mosaic covenant blessings and curses (Leviticus 26:1-46; Deuteronomy 28:1-68). Eliphaz thought that people in right relationship with God would be free from famine (Job 5:20, Job 5:22; see Leviticus 26:4-5, Leviticus 26:10; Deuteronomy 28:4-6, Deuteronomy 28:8, Deuteronomy 28:11-12), war (i.e., death, Job 5:20) and the destruction it causes (Job 5:21, Job 5:22; see Leviticus 26:6-8; Deuteronomy 28:7, Deuteronomy 28:48), and slander. They will even be at peace with wild animals (Job 5:23; see Leviticus 26:6) and the stones of the field. This peace might indicate fertile rather than stony fields (2 Kgs 3:19, 25; Matthew 13:5), or it might symbolize wider harmony with the natural world (see Psalm 91:11-12).
nothing will be missing: See Deuteronomy 28:11-12; cp. Job 1:6-19.
descendants . . . as plentiful as grass: See Genesis 22:17; Leviticus 26:9; Deuteronomy 28:4, Deuteronomy 28:11-12.

Job’s response attacks his counselors (ch Job 6:1-30) and challenges God (ch Job 7:1-21). He excuses his passionate words by referencing the depths of his misery (Job 6:2-3; Job 7:11). Job says that Eliphaz has failed to offer comfort or sympathy as a friend, having chosen instead to haggle over stale theological precepts.

In the Old Testament, arrows are associated with supernatural peril, pestilence, and destructive ills (Job 7:20; Job 16:12-13; Deuteronomy 32:23-24, Deuteronomy 32:42; Psalm 7:12-13; Psalm 38:2; Psalm 64:7; Psalm 91:5-6; Lamentations 2:4; Lamentations 3:12-13; Ezekiel 5:16).
the tasteless white of an egg? Job’s riddle-like complaint probably refers both to Eliphaz’s weak counsel and the detestable situation God had allowed him to endure.
At one time, both Moses and Elijah wished that God would kill them (Numbers 11:15; 1 Kgs 19:4).

Job and his friends might have been bound by a covenant of loyalty and faithfulness (Hebrew khesed; see Genesis 21:23; Exodus 15:13; 1 Chr 16:34) that made them like brothers (Job 6:14-15), protectors (Job 6:21-23), and trusted friends (Job 6:27). If this was the case, Job was accusing his friends of violating their covenant with him.

The city of Tema in the northern Arabian desert was at the junction of roads from Damascus to Mecca and from the Persian Gulf to Aqaba (Isaiah 21:14; Jeremiah 25:23). It might have been named after one of Ishmael’s descendants (Genesis 25:15). It was not the same as Teman, Eliphaz’s home in Edom. • Sheba, located in southwest Arabia, was a market city for precious commodities (Psalm 72:10, Psalm 72:15; Isaiah 60:6; Jeremiah 6:20; Ezekiel 27:22-23; Ezekiel 38:13).
even send an orphan into slavery: Job, the former protector of orphans (Job 31:17, Job 31:21), used a proverbial example of his counselors’ hard-heartedness toward the defenseless (see Job 17:5).
Don’t I know the difference between right and wrong? (literally Can’t my palate discern malice?): Job might have been echoing his earlier comment about a tasteless, revolting diet (Job 6:6-7).
Human life has been a struggle since the Fall (Genesis 3:17; Genesis 5:29; Ecclesiastes 1:2, Ecclesiastes 1:13-14; Ecclesiastes 2:11, Ecclesiastes 2:17; Romans 8:20-22).
A worker was to be paid at the end of each day (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:15), though this did not always happen (Jeremiah 22:13; Malachi 3:5; James 5:4).

Job’s trial might already have gone on for months. • The Hebrew term (‘amal) that runs throughout Job is translated as “misery/miserable” (Job 3:20; Job 11:16; Job 16:2; Job 20:22) or as “trouble” (Job 3:10; Job 4:8; Job 5:6, Job 5:7; Job 15:35).
Job’s reference to maggots signified mortality (Job 25:6) and the rampant corruption of Sheol (Job 17:14; Job 21:26; Job 24:20; see Isaiah 14:11).
Job cried out to God, complaining that life was too brief (Job 7:6-10). This complaint contrasts ironically with his earlier desire that God end it all (Job 6:9).

Those who call upon God to remember are typically seeking covenant mercy (Psalm 35:6; Psalm 106:4). • Job’s declaration that life is but a breath (Hebrew ruakh) meant either that he was one breath away from death or that his life was like a passing wind (Psalm 39:9, Psalm 39:11).
You see me now, but not for long: The Greek Old Testament omitted this verse to avoid the implication that God would be unable to see Job in Sheol (see study note on 7:9).

die (literally go down to Sheol): This is the first explicit mention of Sheol in Job. It is described as a place of rest from earthly pressures and distinctions (Job 3:13-19) and as a dark dwelling place (Job 10:21-22; Job 17:13) deep in the earth (Job 11:8) that is covered in dust (Job 17:16). It is the destiny of all the living (Job 30:23) from which no one can return (Job 10:21; see Genesis 37:25; 2 Sam 12:12).
I cannot keep from speaking: Job echoed Eliphaz’s inability to refrain from words (Job 4:2).

The sea monster (Hebrew yam) and dragon (Hebrew tannin) represent chaotic opposition to God’s orderly creation. In Canaanite mythology, Yam was the primordial sea god and Tannin was a sea monster (Jeremiah 51:34) or a mythological deity of chaos (Psalm 74:13-14). This kind of chaos is also represented in Job as Leviathan (Job 3:8; Isaiah 27:1) or Rahab (Job 9:13; Job 26:12; Isaiah 51:9). The Lord is sovereign over the sea and all that it represents (Job 26:12; Job 38:8-11; Psalm 89:9-10; Jeremiah 5:22).
Job’s sickbed dreams and visions echoed those of Eliphaz (Job 4:12-16).
for my few remaining days: Literally for my days are a vapor (Hebrew hebel); see “All Is ‘Vapor’” Theme Note.

that you should make so much of us: Cp. Psalm 8:4-5, which treats the same thoughts positively. • examine (Hebrew paqad): In Psalm 8:4, the same term means “to honor or care for”; Job used the term ironically, meaning “to be pestered” (cp. “attacked,” Isaiah 26:14).

Won’t you leave me alone (literally How long will you not look away from me): Job sought the opposite of the watchful care that faithful people usually seek (Numbers 6:25; Psalm 27:9; Psalm 69:17; Psalm 80:3, Psalm 80:7, Psalm 80:19; Lamentations 1:9). • to swallow: This is equivalent to “a chance to catch my breath.”

watcher of all humanity: Rather than praising God for his goodness expressed in watchfulness (Deuteronomy 32:10; Psalm 25:21; Proverbs 24:12), Job blamed God for hostile surveillance, which actually characterizes Satan’s activity (Job 1:7). • Why is from the language of lament (see study note on 3:11-24). • your target: See Job 6:4; Lamentations 3:12.

Like Eliphaz, Bildad the Shuhite (see study note on 2:11) believed that Job’s sufferings were God’s retribution (Job 8:3-6, Job 8:13; cp. Job 4:7-8; Job 5:2-3). This counselor revered the wisdom of the past (Job 8:8-10; cp. Job 4:7) and addressed Job with a mixture of instruction (Job 8:3-6, Job 8:8-10; cp. Job 4:12-21; Job 5:9-16) and encouragement (Job 8:5-7, Job 8:20-22; cp. Job 4:6; Job 5:19-26). His point was that Job should quit blustering. He advised Job to repent and allow God’s justice to bring about restoration (Job 8:1-7).
How long? Bildad’s question might be an ironic parody of Job’s question in Job 7:19.

According to Bildad, God does not twist justice, so the death of Job’s children proved that they had sinned against God. Bildad divided people into the blameless (Hebrew tam, Job 8:20; see Job 1:1) and the secretly wicked (Hebrew khanep, Job 8:13). He believed that they could be differentiated by watching what God did to them.
you will end with much: Bildad’s words were more true than he realized (Job 42:12; cp. Job 5:19-26).
Bildad made the case for traditional wisdom by appealing to ancient tradition and history (Deuteronomy 4:32; Jeremiah 18:13).
born but yesterday and know nothing: Bildad suggested that Job’s generation was either born too late to be acquainted with ancient wisdom or was too young to have accumulated it.
Papyrus reeds grow as high as ten to fifteen feet.
To forget God does not mean to have a lapse of memory but to act as if God did not exist (see Psalm 10:4; Psalm 14:1; Zephaniah 1:12) or cannot see (see Job 22:13-17; Psalm 94:7).
In this parable, a plant with roots that grow down through a pile of stones gains stability by becoming entwined with the rocks.

Job responded to Bildad by describing God’s cosmic and judicial power. His speech sounds like a complicated legal case, with a summons and response (Job 9:3, Job 9:14-16, Job 9:19, Job 9:32), the possibility of self-incrimination (Job 9:20), an arbiter (Job 9:33-34), an accusatory question (Job 9:12), a legal sentence (Job 9:22), and a declaration of guilt (Job 9:28-30).
If someone wanted to take God to court: Job later expressed the wish to meet God in court (Job 13:3, Job 13:15, Job 13:23; Job 23:4).

When God moves the mountains and when the foundations of the earth tremble, it is a sign of his presence as lawgiver (Exodus 19:18), judge (Jeremiah 4:24), or rescuer (Psalm 18:7; Isaiah 13:13; Isaiah 29:6).
The Bear (also at Job 38:32) is commonly identified as Arcturus but might also refer to the constellations of Ursa Minor or Leo. • The Pleiades is a group of seven stars (Job 38:31; Amos 5:8).

monsters of the sea (literally the helpers of Rahab): Job personified demonic powers as creatures like this mythical sea monster that represents chaos in ancient literature (Job 26:12; Psalm 89:11; Isaiah 51:9).
with a storm: Perhaps the words translated “with a storm” (bis’arah) are a double entendre with besa‘arah (“for a hair”; i.e., “for the littlest thing”), which would parallel without cause.
Job was indeed innocent (Job 1:1, Job 1:7; Job 2:3), and he maintained this claim throughout the debate (Job 23:11-12; Job 27:5; Job 31:1-40).
The word you makes it clear that this is a prayer, although the phrase O God is not explicit in the Hebrew.
wash myself: Job spoke of cleansing himself with the strongest soap to represent ridding himself of all sin (Job 1:5; cp. Psalm 26:6; Matthew 27:24).

The muddy ditch (literally pit) can refer to the place of the dead (Job 17:14; Job 33:18), so it might allude to the defilement of death. • The filthy clothing of guilt contrasts with the clean clothes of acquittal (Zechariah 3:3-5; see Isaiah 61:10; Isaiah 64:6; Revelation 19:8).
A mediator would not judge God and man but would work to bring them together (see Job 16:19-21).

A succession of images describes God’s role in creating Job. • You formed me with your hands . . . made me from dust: This was how a potter made a vessel (Isaiah 45:9; Jeremiah 18:1-12). Although the potter has incontestable sovereignty over the clay (Isaiah 45:9; Jeremiah 18:5-12; Romans 9:20-25), Job was questioning God. • back to dust: This common motif in Job represents the temporary nature of life (Job 4:19; Job 7:9-10, Job 7:21; Job 14:1-2, Job 14:10; see Genesis 3:19). • You guided my conception and formed me in the womb: The Hebrew terminology (literally You poured me out like milk and curdled me like cheese) evokes graphic images of a newborn baby still covered with the creamy substance called vernix.
Earlier, Job had painted a fairly pleasant picture of Sheol (Job 3:13-19); now he describes it as a land of darkness and utter gloom (see also Job 7:9-10; Job 14:7-22).
Zophar the Naamathite (see study note on 2:11), the most severe of Job’s three friends, dealt only with the issue of sin.

this torrent of words: Verbosity is characteristic of fools (Proverbs 10:8, Job 10:14) and sinners (Proverbs 10:19), but Job was innocent. • mock God: Zophar viewed Job’s words about God’s justice as sinfully sarcastic (Job 10:2-7, Job 10:13-15).
My beliefs are pure: Job was not defining doctrine but defending his own integrity.
punishing you . . . less than you deserve: Zophar believed that calamity indicated divine retribution for sins (cp. Job 34:36).
No one can discover everything about the Almighty (literally find out the limits of the Almighty), who is beyond the limits of the heavens, underworld, land, and sea (Job 11:8-9).

Zophar laid out three conditions for restoration (Job 11:15): (1) prepare your heart, in an inward act that is not just a ritual; (2) lift up your hands, a symbolic gesture of prayer, appeal (Exodus 9:29; Proverbs 1:24; Isaiah 1:15), or surrender; (3) leave all iniquity, not by sacrifice and remorse, but by quitting the sin (cp. Hebrews 11:6; James 4:8; James 5:16).
In his longest speech thus far, Job addresses not only Zophar’s remarks but the entire first round of speeches.

ask the animals . . . birds . . . earth . . . fish: Job believed that the reason for his misery was obvious and that even nature would understand it (Proverbs 6:6). Later, God directed Job’s attention to the animal kingdom to convince Job that he did not understand (Job 38:1–40:24).
A switch from you (plural in Job 12:2-3) to you (singular here) probably indicates that Job is directing his comments to Zophar.

from the hand of the Lord: This is the only place in the dialogues (chs Job 3:1–27:23; Job 29:1–37:24) that the Hebrew Yahweh (“the Lord”) is used. For Job, the dispute was not about who caused his misery but why it happened.
the mouth distinguishes between foods: See Job 6:6-7.
Wisdom belongs to the aged: Job’s friends defended this opinion (Job 8:8-10; Job 15:10; Job 32:6-9), but Job questioned it (Job 12:20).

stripped of good judgment: The NLT adds “of good judgment” for clarity. In this image, God metaphorically strips leaders of their abilities. It could also refer to being stripped of the symbols of office or to becoming naked captives (Job 12:18-19).

When God removes the royal robe of kings, he takes away the symbols of their authority (cp. Job 19:9). It could also be translated as “God loosens the bonds of kings,” referring to the bondage they have imposed on others.
The priests are figuratively stripped of status (the NLT adds “of status” for clarity) or are actually stripped of priestly robes; they might even be naked captives (Job 12:18).
pours disgrace upon princes: Cp. Psalm 107:40. • disarms (literally looses the belt of): The strong are no longer girded for battle.

uncovers mysteries (literally uncovers the deeps): This phrase might allude to Zophar’s words that God’s knowledge is “deeper than the underworld” (Job 11:8). • darkness . . . deepest gloom: The Old Testament often describes God as dwelling in darkness (1 Kgs 8:12; 2 Chr 6:1) and as manifesting himself through darkness (2 Sam 22:10, 12; Psalm 18:9, Psalm 18:11), as when he gave the law at Sinai (Deuteronomy 4:11; Deuteronomy 5:22-23) or when he comes in judgment (Zephaniah 1:15).

Cp. Daniel 2:21. • strips kings of understanding: See Job 12:18; cp. Daniel 4:23, Daniel 4:32-33. • He . . . leaves them wandering in a pathless wasteland like the princes in Psalm 107:40 (see Job 12:21).
Perhaps foolish counsel made the kings stagger like drunkards (Job 12:17; see Isaiah 19:14); it resulted from “drinking” God’s wrath (Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15-27).
Job appealed to experience, as his comforters had done (Job 3:12-17; Job 5:2).
defending God with lies: False witnesses were forbidden even if speaking on God’s behalf (Exodus 20:16).
Ashes are worthless (cp. Isaiah 44:20).
Job had contemplated finding an arbiter to remove God’s heavy hand (Job 9:33-34). Eliphaz had urged Job to accept God’s chastening (Job 5:17).

Job wanted God to summon him, and then Job would answer in his own defense; or Job would speak to God, and then God would reply to substantiate the charges against Job. Since God did not take the first option, Job initiated the second one (Job 13:23). Eventually, God did summon Job (Job 38:1-3; Job 40:1-2), and Job was unable to reply (Job 40:3-5).

God can turn away in wrath (Deuteronomy 31:18; Isaiah 54:8; Jeremiah 33:5) or refuse to show friendship (Psalm 30:7; Psalm 69:17; Psalm 102:2). • Job, perhaps playing on his own name (’iyyob), denied that he was God’s enemy (’oyeb).

In the Old Testament, dry straw is a common image for what can be blown away (“chaff,” Psalm 83:13; Isaiah 40:24; Jeremiah 13:24) or burned (Exodus 15:7; Isaiah 47:14; Malachi 4:1; see also “dry grass,” Isaiah 5:24; Isaiah 33:11), or for what is weak (Job 41:20-21) and trifling (Isaiah 41:2).
The flower is an image of life’s brevity (Psalm 90:5-6; Psalm 103:15-16; Isaiah 40:6-7). • A shadow passes swiftly (1 Chr 29:15; Psalm 102:11).
keep an eye on: Job lamented God’s relentless surveillance (Job 7:8, Job 7:17-20; Job 10:6, Job 10:14; Job 13:27).

do not rise again: Job himself did not have even the minimal evidence of resurrection found in the Old Testament (2 Kgs 13:21; Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; cp. Job 19:25). • Job was not focusing on the end of the universe when the heavens will be no more (Psalm 102:25-26; Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 51:6; Hebrews 1:10-12) but on the eternity of the heavens (Psalm 148:6; cp. Psalm 72:5, Psalm 72:7, Psalm 72:17; Psalm 89:29, Psalm 89:37). His phrase refers to the permanency of death.
Since the grave is a permanent abode (Job 14:10-12, see Job 3:13-19; Job 7:6-10; Job 10:20-22), Job could not even fulfill his request from Job 13:20-21 by hiding temporarily in the grave.
guard my steps: Here, Job refers to God’s providential care (Job 10:12) rather than to his surveillance (Job 13:27; Job 14:3).
If sins are sealed in a pouch they do not await a time of reckoning (Deuteronomy 32:34-35; Hosea 13:12)—they are hidden forever. Job was requesting acquittal.

Job no longer saw Sheol as a haven (Job 3:17-19; Job 14:13-17). The Old Testament usually depicts the dead as being without feeling (Psalm 88:12; Ecclesiastes 9:5; cp. Isaiah 50:11; Isaiah 66:24); the doctrine that the dead suffer painfully is clearer in the New Testament (Luke 16:23, Luke 16:28; Revelation 14:11).
In this second round of speeches, Job’s friends focus on the fate of the wicked and imply that Job’s condition shows he has sinned.

You are nothing but a windbag (literally You fill your belly with the east wind): Since the east wind was hot, it might represent heated (Exodus 14:21; Hosea 13:15; Jonah 4:8) or violent (Job 27:21; Jeremiah 18:17) speech.
Your own mouth condemns you: Job feared that this would happen (Job 9:20; see Matthew 26:65).
When the Lord himself later issued a similar challenge, Job found it convicting (Job 38:1-11).
The book’s readers know about God’s secret council (Job 1:6-12; Job 2:1-6; see 1 Kgs 22:19-20; Psalm 89:5-7), but Job and his company did not.
Aged, gray-haired men claim a monopoly on wisdom (Job 8:8-10; Job 12:20; see Job 12:2).
What has weakened your vision (literally Why do your eyes blink): This sentence might be a metaphor for unbelief, or it could indicate winking like a schemer or blinking in disbelief.
Can any mortal be pure? Eliphaz repeated himself (Job 4:17-19) and Job (Job 7:17; Job 14:4). • anyone born of a woman: Both “mortal” and “born of woman” imply weakness.
The heavens, traditionally associated with purity (Exodus 24:10), were not absolutely pure; they had been defiled, perhaps by rebellious angels (Job 1:6-7).
before any foreigners arrived: Eliphaz’s contempt for foreign ideas is ironic because wisdom literature has a more international flavor than is characteristic of other Old Testament writings.

The wicked also suffer everything that happened to Job (see Job 1:16-19)—attacks by marauders (Job 15:21), loss of possessions (Job 15:29), crumbled houses (Job 15:28), and fire (Job 15:30, Job 15:34).

Although Eliphaz generalized the terror that the wicked experience, Job had undergone similar experiences (Job 3:25; Job 6:4; Job 9:34; Job 13:11, Job 13:21; Job 23:15; Job 27:20; Job 30:15). Bildad (Job 18:11, Job 18:14) and Zophar (Job 20:25) spoke of more terror to come. • The Sabeans and Chaldeans were examples of the destroyer (Job 1:13-17), but this could refer to any destructive agent (Job 1:18-19). Destroyers might be agents of Satan (1 Cor 10:10; Revelation 9:11) or divine agents that punish wickedness (Exodus 12:23; 2 Sam 24:16; 2 Chr 32:21; Acts 12:23; Hebrews 11:28). Eliphaz meant the latter.
for fear they will be murdered (literally he is marked for the sword): The wicked might be killed by murder or by the sword of God’s wrath.

They wander around, saying, “Where can I find bread?”: Like the wicked (Job 15:20), Job either experienced hunger (see Job 15:27) or (following the Greek Old Testament) had been “appointed to be food for a vulture,” which would parallel “marked for the sword” (Job 15:22).
Job had complained earlier that God was treating him like a formidable foe (Job 7:19-21; Job 13:24).

The burning sun (literally The flame) might be the scorching sun or a flame of judgment from God (Job 15:34, see Numbers 16:31-35; Psalm 106:17-18; Ezekiel 20:47). • The breath of God might be a desert wind or a more direct theophany (a manifestation of God’s presence) that caused the burning of Job 15:34.
The flame of judgment (Job 15:30) will burn the unjust gain of the godless.
Job might have wanted to shake his head in mockery or in horror (2 Kgs 19:21; Psalm 22:7; Psalm 109:25; Isaiah 37:22; Jeremiah 18:16; Lamentations 2:15; Matthew 27:39).
Job’s family here means his extended household, including his servants (Job 1:15-19).

jeer and laugh at me: Job was the subject of mockery (cp. Psalm 35:21; Isaiah 57:4; Lamentations 2:16; Lamentations 3:46). • To slap the cheek was less an act of violence (Psalm 3:7; Micah 5:1) than an insult (1 Kgs 22:24; Isaiah 50:6; Lamentations 3:30; Matthew 26:67).
took me by the neck: This might refer to a wild animal with its prey (see Job 16:9), but it is more likely a military image that signaled defeat (Genesis 49:8; Psalm 18:40).
pierce me: Literally pierce my kidneys. • my blood: Literally my gall. The picture is of wounds to vital organs.

Again and again he smashes against me: Job pictures himself as a fortress that God is besieging. Job saw God as a warrior (cp. Exodus 15:3; Psalm 24:8) who did not defend him or offer him salvation (Jeremiah 20:11; Zephaniah 3:17) but attacked him as though he were dangerous (Job 6:12; see Isaiah 42:13).

Since Job insisted on his innocence, his wearing burlap (literally I sewed on burlap) was a sign of mourning, not penitence. Perhaps it was attached to indicate that he would never remove it because he could never be consoled (Genesis 37:34-35). • My pride lies in the dust (literally I have buried my horn in the dust): A horn symbolized dignity and power (1 Sam 2:1; Psalm 75:4-5; Psalm 89:17, Psalm 89:24; Psalm 92:10; Psalm 112:9; Psalm 148:14); cutting it off inflicted degrading humiliation (Psalm 75:10; Jeremiah 48:25; Zechariah 1:12).

done no wrong (or done no violence; Hebrew lo’-khamas): If violence is the meaning, Job was possibly denying that he was a formidable warrior who should be attacked (Job 16:12-14; see also Isaiah 59:6; Jonah 3:8). • Contrary to Eliphaz’s charge (Job 15:4-5) and Bildad’s assumption (Job 8:6), Job’s prayer was pure because he was innocent (Genesis 20:5; Isaiah 59:3).
Job’s blood would cry out that he had been innocent and that he had suffered undeservedly (cp. Genesis 4:10-11; Isaiah 26:21; Ezekiel 24:7-8).
Job expected his suffering to prove fatal (Job 7:7, Job 7:21; Job 10:20-22); he pleaded with God to reveal his innocence even if he died first.

my witness is in heaven: Job wished for a benevolent third party who would mediate between him and God (see Job 9:32-35). Job wanted an advocate from heaven (Job 16:19; cp. Zechariah 3:1) who would eventually stand on the earth (Job 19:25; cp. 1 Sam 24:15; John 14:16, John 14:26; John 15:26; John 16:7; 1 Jn 2:1).
My spirit is crushed: This can refer to a properly contrite attitude (Psalm 51:17), but more often it connotes an unbearably sad heart (Proverbs 18:14).

surrounded by mockers: Laments typically describe mockery as the response of the wicked to the distress of the righteous (Psalm 22:7; Psalm 69:10-12; Psalm 89:50-52). In wisdom literature, mockery is directed against the right behavior (Proverbs 1:22; Proverbs 9:7).

defend my innocence, O God (literally please keep my pledge with yourself): A pledge (Hebrew ‘erabon) can be a deposit guaranteeing payment (Genesis 38:17-20; Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:10-14; see Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 27:13), so this might suggest atonement. It might also be another reference to Job’s desire for an advocate to plead his case (see study note on Job 16:19-21).
To spit in someone’s face was even more insulting than a slap (Job 16:10) because spit made the person unclean (Numbers 12:14).
Some scholars view these verses as being out of place, but perhaps Job was ironically quoting his opponents’ words.
Job gave up on his comforters (Job 6:15-21; Job 13:4-5; Job 16:2-3; cp. Job 12:2) and believed he would die a hopeless death.
to the grave (Hebrew to Sheol): The realm of the dead was visualized as a house (Job 30:23; Psalm 49:11; Ecclesiastes 12:5).
my father . . . mother . . . sister: This bitter parody of a family reunion in a graveyard shows how Job envisioned his impending death.
the grave (literally the bars of Sheol): Sheol—the abode of the dead—was seen as having a barred gate, allowing no escape.
How long before you stop talking? Bildad addressed Job in the plural, perhaps meaning “people like you.”
The light of the wicked will be snuffed out could be a metaphor for a life of confused darkness (Proverbs 4:19); more likely, it indicates an early death (Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 24:20).
The stride that is shortened is the opposite of walking and running in the blessed life (Proverbs 4:12).
A series of hunting devices illustrates the biblical principle of retribution (see study note on 34:11).
Bildad applies the biblical principle of retribution (Job 18:8-10) to Job, as do Eliphaz (Job 15:21-23) and Zophar (Job 20:25).
death devours: Isaiah later reversed the figure and saw the Lord as swallowing up death (Isaiah 25:8; see 1 Cor 15:54).
The image of burning sulfur recalls the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24) and suggests the fate of all the wicked (Psalm 11:6; Revelation 19:20; Revelation 21:8).
Being forgotten by those who come later is a familiar curse against the wicked (see Job 18:19; Psalm 34:16; Psalm 109:13; Proverbs 10:7).

This curse of childlessness (see Job 18:16; Psalm 109:13; Isaiah 14:21-22) and Bildad’s earlier cruelty (Job 8:4) show that he regarded Job’s condition as the just reward for his wickedness (Job 1:18-19).
in the west . . . in the east: These phrases might refer to people from times past and times to come or to people from various places.
Bildad kept implying that Job had rejected God (Job 15:4, Job 15:13, Job 15:25).
The number ten did not represent a specific count but an indefinite large number (e.g., Genesis 31:7; Leviticus 26:26; Numbers 14:22; Daniel 1:20).

Job was convinced that justice had been delayed (Job 19:7) and that God had wronged him (Job 19:8-12). Later, Elihu (Job 34:12) and God himself (Job 40:2) disagreed. • capturing me in his net: Job might have been responding to Bildad’s accusation (Job 18:8-10).
Help! (literally Violence!): Cp. Jeremiah 20:8; Habakkuk 1:2-3. • no one answers: See Psalm 22:2; Lamentations 3:8; Habakkuk 1:2-3.
blocked my way: See Job 3:23; Job 13:27; Psalm 88:8; Lamentations 3:7, Lamentations 3:9.
stripped me of my honor: See Job 12:17-19; Job 29:7-14, Job 29:20.
my own family: Job might have been referring to his tribal line, his parents, his own children, or his siblings.
Those I loved have turned against me: See Job 2:11; also Job 6:14-15, Job 6:21-23, Job 6:27; cp. Psalm 41:9; Psalm 55:12-14, Psalm 55:20.
escaped death by the skin of my teeth: This is an idiom for a narrow escape; the Hebrew could also mean that Job was reduced to a skeleton with a toothy skull.
The hand of God had struck Job through the permission he gave to Satan (Job 1:11; Job 2:5).
persecute (literally pursue): Job complained that God had tracked him like a hunter (Job 10:16) or a warrior (Job 16:13).
Job wanted his words . . . inscribed on a monument, not in a book; Job desired a permanent record of his claim to innocence in response to Bildad’s assertion that he would be forgotten (Job 18:17).

Job’s faith in a Redeemer could find fulfillment only in Christ; the same was true of his request for an advocate (Job 9:33) and a witness in heaven (Job 16:19). The term “Redeemer” (Hebrew go’el) comes from both criminal and civil law. An individual could redeem or avenge wrongful bloodshed (Numbers 35:12-18) or redeem lost property, perhaps by buying back a slave or marrying the heir’s widow (Leviticus 25:25, Leviticus 25:47-49; Leviticus 27:11-13; Ruth 3:13). The Old Testament knew the Lord as redeemer (Exodus 6:6; Psalm 19:14; Psalm 103:4; Proverbs 23:10-11; Isaiah 43:1 [“ransomed”]; Isaiah 54:5); New Testament believers know the Redeemer as the Lord Jesus Christ (Ephesians 1:7, Ephesians 1:14; Hebrews 9:12; 1 Pet 1:18). Job wanted his Redeemer to declare his innocence (see Job 1:1 and corresponding study note).
Job had faith that he would be vindicated even if death came first.

I will see him for myself: The thought is the same as the psalmist’s in “when I awake” (Psalm 17:15). For Job, this hope could only be fulfilled in seeing God at the end of time (Matthew 5:8; 1 Cor 13:12; 1 Jn 3:2; Revelation 1:7) in transformed flesh (1 Cor 15:43-53; Philippians 3:21).

Given the biblical principles against bearing false witness (Job 13:7-11; see Matthew 7:1-2; James 4:11-12), Job warned his friends that they should fear God’s judgment. They did eventually face his judgment, but they also received mercy (Job 42:7-8).
thrown away like their own dung: Cp. 1 Kgs 14:9-11; 2 Kgs 9:36-37; Psalm 83:10; Jeremiah 8:1-2.
Because stolen riches are ill-gotten, they provide no lasting benefit (Job 20:18-21).
poisonous venom . . . cobras . . . viper: In the end, the wicked are no longer deadly to others (Matthew 3:7; Romans 3:13) but only to themselves (Proverbs 23:29-35).
The streams of olive oil and rivers of milk and honey signify superabundant blessing (Exodus 5:19; Deuteronomy 27:3; Joel 3:18).
Like the grave or death (Proverbs 27:20; Proverbs 30:15-16), the wicked are always greedy and never satisfied (Ecclesiastes 5:19; Isaiah 57:20-21; Habakkuk 2:5).
The wicked cannot escape trouble (cp. Isaiah 24:17-18; Jeremiah 15:2-3; Amos 5:19; Amos 9:1-2). When they try to escape one threat, they fall victim to another.

terrors of death: Although the words “of death” are not in the Hebrew, they are implied because the arrowhead glistens with blood (literally with gall), indicating a deadly hit on a vital organ (Job 6:4; Job 16:13; Psalm 7:12).

Images such as deepest darkness and wildfire are often associated with God’s presence (Deuteronomy 4:11; Deuteronomy 5:22-23; Hebrews 12:18) and especially with his judgment (Exodus 9:23-24; Exodus 10:21-29).
heavens . . . will testify: Cp. Deuteronomy 4:26; Deuteronomy 30:19; Deuteronomy 31:28.

Job’s friends insisted that they were delivering God’s own message of comfort (Job 15:11), but Job found no comfort in their words (Job 16:2), so he asked for the consolation of their attentive silence (see Job 13:5).

When I think about what I am saying: Job was dismayed by his horrible task of complaining against God (Job 13:3, Job 13:15-16, Job 13:22; Job 23:1-5) and discussing his terrors (Job 6:4; Job 27:20; Job 30:15). • My body trembles: This reaction resembles that of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 1:5; Habakkuk 3:16), Ezekiel (Ezekiel 3:14), and Daniel (Daniel 8:27; Daniel 10:8-9).

In spite of assertions by Eliphaz (Job 5:4), Bildad (Job 18:19), and Zophar (Job 20:10), Job noted that the wicked enjoy children and grandchildren, which should be the reward of the righteous (Proverbs 17:6) but was apparently not going to be his own reward (Job 1:18-19; but see Job 42:13-16).
light of the wicked never seems to be extinguished: Job countered Bildad (Job 18:5-6, Job 18:18) and standard wisdom (Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 20:20; Job 24:20; see God’s remarks, Job 38:15).

you say: Job was quoting and rebutting his friends’ arguments. • God will punish their children: These were the words of Eliphaz (Job 5:4) and Zophar (Job 20:10), but Job thought God should punish the ones who sin (see Ezekiel 18:19-20).

The rhetorical answer is that no one can teach a lesson to God (Isaiah 40:13-14; Isaiah 45:9; Romans 11:34; 1 Cor 2:16). • The most powerful might refer to angels or demons (1 Cor 6:3; 2 Pet 2:4; Jude 1:6; Revelation 20:1-3) or, more likely, to the powerful on earth (Job 34:17-19).
vigorous and fit (literally the marrow of his bones [is] moist): Bones were thought to be the seat of health.
in bitter poverty: Job repeatedly complained about the apparent futility of existence (Job 3:20; Job 7:11; Job 9:18; Job 10:1).
eaten by the same maggots: Cp. Job 17:14; Isaiah 14:11; see Job 19:26.
houses have vanished because of their sins: Job was echoing Bildad (Job 8:22), Eliphaz (Job 15:34), and Zophar (Job 20:26).
the earth gives sweet repose: Job viewed death as a relief (Job 3:17-18).
They told lies about Job (Job 13:4) and about God (Job 42:7).
In this third round of speeches, Job’s friends explicitly accuse Job of being among the wicked and sharing their fate.

Eliphaz did not understand that God would gain pleasure from Job’s righteousness (Job 1:8; Job 2:3), as he does from every righteous person (1 Chr 29:17; Psalm 147:10-11; Proverbs 11:1, Proverbs 11:20; Proverbs 12:22). God would also gain glory from Job’s steadfast faith, which emphasized the lie behind Satan’s challenge (Job 1:9-12; Job 2:4-6). • Job steadfastly claimed that he was perfect (Job 23:10-12), as did God himself (Job 1:1, Job 1:8; Job 2:3).

Demanding clothing as security for lent money was forbidden by the law and condemned by the prophets (Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:10-13; Ezekiel 18:7-8; Amos 2:8). In contrast, Job had provided clothing for the poor (Job 31:19-20).

The Old Testament gives Israel the responsibility of caring for widows and orphans (Deuteronomy 10:18; Deuteronomy 14:29) and repeatedly condemns their neglect as the worst of social evils (Exodus 22:22-24; Deuteronomy 27:19). Job agreed that it was wicked (Job 24:3, Job 24:21) but claimed that he was innocent (Job 29:12-13; Job 31:16-18, Job 31:21).
That’s why: Job had not claimed that God can’t see, but others have (Psalm 10:11; Psalm 73:11; Psalm 94:7).
I will have nothing to do with that kind of thinking: Eliphaz threw Job’s words back at him (Job 21:16).

The righteous will be happy to see the wicked destroyed: They will be glad to see justice done and injustices avenged (see also Psalm 58:10-11; Revelation 19:1-4). Eliphaz’s sentiment neglected God’s desire that sinful people repent (see Ezekiel 33:11).

The term instructions (Hebrew torah, “law,” Deuteronomy 17:11), used in Job only here, frequently refers to the Pentateuch (Genesis—Deuteronomy). • Listen . . . store: See Deuteronomy 4:1-2; Deuteronomy 6:6-9; Psalm 119:11; Proverbs 2:1-9. Job had done this (Job 23:12).

return to the Almighty: Bildad (Job 8:5-6) and Zophar (Job 11:13-14) had already misapplied this biblical principle (Isaiah 55:6-7; Hosea 14:1-2; Zechariah 1:3; Acts 26:20), and now Eliphaz also misapplies it.

precious gold (literally Ophir): Ophir was probably located in southern Arabia (see 1 Kgs 9:28; 22:48). The gold of Ophir was the standard in fine gold (Isaiah 13:12); queens wore it at weddings (Psalm 45:9).
God promises to be his people’s treasure (Psalm 16:5; Isaiah 33:6; Matthew 19:21; Mark 10:21); although they possess nothing, they will be rich (2 Cor 6:10; James 2:5).

Ironically, Job will pray, God will hear, and Eliphaz will reap the benefits (Job 42:8). • you will fulfill your vows: Vows were often stimulated by repentance and forgiveness (Hosea 14:2; Jonah 1:16; Jonah 2:9) and when seeking divine intervention (Judges 11:29-40; 1 Sam 1:1-28). Vows are binding (Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:23; Psalm 22:25; Psalm 61:5, Psalm 61:8; Psalm 116:14, Psalm 116:18; Ecclesiastes 5:4-5).

This difficult text probably conveys the effectiveness of a righteous man’s prayer. The principle (Psalm 34:15, Psalm 34:17; Psalm 145:18; Proverbs 15:8, Job 15:29; James 5:16) is illustrated throughout Scripture (see, e.g., Genesis 18:23-32; Genesis 19:29; Genesis 20:7, Genesis 20:17; Genesis 32:28; Exodus 9:28-32; Exodus 17:11; Exodus 32:10-14; Romans 5:19).
Job dropped the doubt he had expressed earlier (Job 9:14-20, Job 9:32) and here expressed confidence that he could successfully present his complaint.

present my arguments: Job wanted to make his case with God (Job 13:3, Job 13:18, Job 13:22; Job 16:21; Job 31:35); Abraham pled directly with God regarding Sodom (Genesis 18:25-32), and Moses did the same for Israel (Exodus 32:12-13; Numbers 14:13-19).

Earlier, Job had believed that God was too strong for him to summon (Job 9:19), so he had requested an arbiter (Job 9:33-34) and asked God not to terrify him (Job 13:21). Here he expressed more hope that God would grant him a fair hearing. • acquitted: Job did not want to be pardoned as a guilty man but to be declared innocent (Job 13:18; see Psalm 17:2-3; Psalm 26:1-3).

tests me: Job did not want the kind of chastising that would cleanse him like a refiner’s fire (Proverbs 17:3; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:2-3). He wanted an examination that would prove that he had been as pure as gold and did not need to amend his life (Job 22:23).
No one can change God’s mind (Job 9:12-13; Job 11:10; Job 12:14; Job 34:29; Numbers 23:19-20; James 1:17).

terrified in his presence: See Psalm 77:3; Psalm 88:16; Psalm 119:120. • Job had complained earlier of being plunged into darkness (Job 19:8); Eliphaz (Job 15:22; Job 22:1) and Bildad (Job 18:6, Job 18:18) ascribed this fate to the wicked.

bring . . . to judgment (literally set times): The times for God’s judgment are set (Ecclesiastes 3:17; Ecclesiastes 8:6; Daniel 2:21; Luke 21:22-24), but they are not known to us (Acts 1:7). They will be revealed at the proper moment (1 Thes 5:1-28; 1 Tim 6:15).
The law, wisdom literature, and prophecy all condemned the moving of boundary markers (Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 27:17; Proverbs 22:28; Proverbs 23:10; see study note on Hos 5:10).
This inventory of criminal behaviors focuses first on crimes against the weak (Job 24:2-12) and then on the criminals themselves (Job 24:13-17).
The law did not allow seizing necessary belongings as security or collateral for a loan (Job 22:6-9; Deuteronomy 24:6, Deuteronomy 24:10-13, Deuteronomy 24:17-21).

glean in the vineyards of the wicked: Job was depicting the desperate condition of the poor. If their fields had been stolen like Naboth’s vineyard (Job 24:2; see 1 Kgs 21:1-29), the poor would harvest for the thieving owners what should have been their own crops; instead of owning the whole crop, they would get just the leftover pickings for themselves. Perhaps the point is that the poor were forced to glean from the fields of wicked people who left no gleanings (Leviticus 19:10; Leviticus 23:22), instead of being able to glean from the righteous, who leave something for the poor (Leviticus 19:9-10; Leviticus 23:22; Ruth 2:1-23).
Unjust lenders sometimes left debtors without clothing or covering, which they had seized as collateral on loans (Job 22:6; Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:11-13; Amos 2:8).
widow’s child . . . security for a loan: See 2 Kgs 4:1; Nehemiah 5:1-5; Matthew 18:25.

without being allowed to taste it: These words, which are not in the original text, are implied by the parallel with starving and suffer from thirst. • To force workers to tread in the winepress as they suffer from thirst violates the principle of letting workers enjoy some of the produce they are harvesting (see Deuteronomy 25:4; cp. 2 Tim 2:6).

ignores their moaning: It appeared to Job that contrary to God’s own character (Exodus 2:23-24; Psalm 12:5), God neither relieved the plight of the wronged (Job 24:2-12) nor hindered the wicked from harming their victims (Job 24:13-17).

These sentiments appear to oppose Job’s observations, so some scholars suggest that they were the words of Bildad or Zophar. However, Job might have been pronouncing curses on the wicked, sarcastically quoting his friends’ views, or saying that the fate of the wicked presented by Eliphaz (Job 5:2-7; Job 15:17-25), Bildad (Job 8:8-19; Job 18:5-21), and Zophar (Job 20:4-29) also overtakes the righteous (Job 21:23-26).

Eliphaz had said that it is nearly impossible to be innocent or pure (Job 4:17-19; Job 15:14-16), and then only after suffering (Job 22:21-23). Bildad claimed that only the totally blameless could hope to be pure (Job 8:20).

Job’s friends had not helped him (Job 12:2; Job 16:4). Bildad’s denial that acquittal was possible hit Job’s most sensitive nerve (Job 10:1-7; Job 13:3, Job 13:13-19; Job 16:18-21; Job 19:23-27; Job 23:2-7).
Eliphaz (Job 4:15), Zophar (Job 20:3), and Elihu (Job 32:18; Job 33:4) all claimed to be prompted by the proper spirit (see Jeremiah 29:8-9; 1 Cor 12:10; 1 Jn 4:1).
The underworld (Hebrew Sheol), the abode of all the dead, is located beneath the waters of the sea. • The place of destruction (Hebrew Abaddon) existed specifically for the wicked.

The Hebrew tsapon (“north,” Genesis 13:14) sometimes refers to the northern mountain of the Canaanite gods (the Canaanite equivalent of Olympus); here the NLT understands it to refer to the sky, stretched out over empty space (see Genesis 1:6-8; Psalm 104:2-3; Isaiah 40:22-23).
created the horizon: See Genesis 1:6-10; Psalm 104:6-9; Proverbs 8:29.

Mountains at the edge of the horizon might be the foundations (or “pillars,” Judges 16:25-26) of heaven or the earth (Job 9:6). They were thought to reach from below the waters of the sea (Jonah 2:6) and up to the clouds to support the vaults of heaven.

the sea grew calm (cp. Exodus 14:21; Mark 4:39): Or the sea was stirred up (cp. Isaiah 51:15; Jeremiah 31:35). In either interpretation, God performed a miracle on behalf of his people. • crushed the great sea monster: God’s dominance over the sea demythologized popular beliefs about the sea’s divinity. See also Psalm 74:13-14; Psalm 89:9-10; Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9-10.

His Spirit (or wind): God’s authority clears the skies after a storm (Job 26:12). • The gliding serpent corresponds to Yam and Rahab (see study note on 7:12); it provides background for the image of Satan as a dragon (Isaiah 27:1; also Psalm 74:13-14; see Genesis 3:15; Romans 16:20; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2).
Job continued speaking, no longer responding to the three friends but returning to the themes of his opening statement (Job 3:1-26).

The Bible permits a vow by the living God (Ruth 3:13; 1 Sam 20:21; 25:26; 1 Kgs 17:1; 18:15; Jeremiah 4:2), although sometimes it is done foolishly or falsely (1 Sam 14:39, 45; Jeremiah 5:2). • Elihu later criticized Job for saying that God had taken away his rights (Job 34:5). • embittered . . . soul (Job 7:11; Job 10:1; Job 21:25): Cp. Naomi (Ruth 1:20-21) and the widow from Shunem after the loss of her son (2 Kgs 4:27).

Job considered it profane and reprehensible to concede that his friends were right. Condemning the innocent, as they were doing to him, was an abomination (Exodus 23:7; Proverbs 6:16-19; Proverbs 17:15).
Some interpreters see a new speech here and ascribe it to Zophar because otherwise Zophar has no speech in this cycle.

This section is a self-contained speech. No speaker is listed, so it could be a continuation of the preceding words. However, some consider this a poetic interlude by the author of Job that sums up the argument to this point, emphasizes the failure of human wisdom, and lays the foundation for the Lord’s speeches.
Miners melted rock by burning a fire in a mine for days or even weeks to melt out the ore. Some alternated fire with cold water to split the rocks.
Wisdom does not originate among the living. God is the source of true wisdom (Job 28:23-28).
The metals, gemstones, and glass listed here were precious in the ancient world, but the speaker says that wisdom is much more precious than wealth.
When God looks throughout the whole earth (Job 28:23), he sees his own wisdom expressed in his creation. God later showcased his wisdom for Job when he took him on a cosmic tour (chs Job 38:1–41:34).
fear of the Lord (Hebrew, ’adonay): In Job, this name for God appears only here, which might be one argument for understanding ch Job 28:1-28 as the narrator’s own poem.

Job contrasts his former happiness, honor, and wealth (ch Job 29:1-25) with his loss of social dignity and divine friendship (ch Job 30:1-31). He concludes his speech with wide-ranging oaths of innocence (ch Job 31:1-40).

Although elsewhere Job uses the Hebrew shamar to describe what he perceived as God’s oppressive surveillance (Job 10:14; Job 13:27; Job 14:16), here it refers to God’s kindly care (“watch(es) over,” Psalm 121:3-8).
The city gate was a town’s administrative center (see Ruth 4:1-2, Ruth 4:11).
Job described his righteousness in royal terms. A robe is a common biblical image for righteousness (Psalm 132:9; Isaiah 59:17; Isaiah 61:10; Romans 13:14; Revelation 19:8).
Job actively searched out and assisted strangers who needed help.

after a long, good life (literally after I have counted my days like sand): Job thought the length of his years would signify God’s blessing, like the great number of Abraham’s offspring (Genesis 15:5; Genesis 32:12) or the abundance of Joseph’s supplies in Egypt (Genesis 41:49).

In the past, Job had comforted those who mourned (Job 4:3-4). This verse is a prophetic mandate closely associated with the work of the Messiah (Isaiah 40:1; Isaiah 61:1-3; Luke 4:18-19; cp. 2 Cor 1:3-4).

In the past, the most honorable members of society spoke well of Job (Job 29:11); now, the least honorable mocked him (Job 30:1) and spit in his face (Job 30:10). Cp. Psalm 35:15; Psalm 69:12; Mark 14:65; Mark 15:17-20.

live in frightening ravines, in caves and among the rocks: The wretched life of Job’s mockers resembled Israel’s situation under Midianite oppression (Judges 6:2), David’s life as he fled from Saul (1 Sam 22:1-2), and Elijah’s life as he awaited the Lord’s instruction (1 Kgs 17:3-8).
They taunt me! See also Job 17:6; cp. Psalm 69:12; Lamentations 3:14, Lamentations 3:63.

won’t come near me: See also Job 19:13-15; cp. Psalm 88:8; Proverbs 19:7; Matthew 26:56. • To spit in someone’s face was to display revulsion or contempt (Deuteronomy 25:9; Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 26:67; Matthew 27:30; Mark 14:65).

The series of images presented here is drawn from a military advance against a fortified city. Job had already used this image for God’s attack on him (Job 19:10-12). • The word translated traps might refer to siege ramps raised against a city’s walls.
terror: See also Job 6:4; Job 7:14; cp. Psalm 88:15.

God grabs . . . the collar of my coat: The Hebrew in this verse is difficult to translate; it could mean that Job feels like he is in a chokehold and is about to be thrown into the mud (cp. Job 30:19).
dust and ashes: Earlier, Job was sitting “among the ashes” in anguish (Job 2:8); later, he would “sit in dust and ashes to show . . . repentance” (Job 42:6).
you don’t answer: This was Job’s frequent complaint (Job 9:16; Job 19:7; Job 23:2-9; Job 31:35), which God soon answered (Job 38:1).
Job felt tossed into the whirlwind and blown about like worthless straw or chaff (Job 9:17; Job 21:18; Job 27:21; Psalm 1:4; Isaiah 17:13).
Before his testing began, Job had been respected in the public square (Job 29:7-10, Job 29:21-25); he helped others who were in need (Job 29:11-17).

I am considered: Job might have been expressing what he thought of himself, how others viewed him, or both. • By claiming that he was a brother to jackals and a companion to owls, Job might have been describing himself as in the throes of lament (Micah 1:8). Jackals were associated with desolation or ruin (see Psalm 63:10; Isaiah 13:22; Isaiah 34:13; Isaiah 35:7; Jeremiah 9:11; Jeremiah 10:22; Jeremiah 49:33; Jeremiah 51:37; Lamentations 5:18; Ezekiel 13:4; Malachi 1:3).
The skin of a person who lived in comfortable circumstances was protected from the sun and wind; dark skin indicated physical and social decline (Lamentations 4:8; Lamentations 5:10).

Job’s covenant with his eyes included a self-cursing oath (cp. Matthew 5:28-29). Perhaps lust of the eyes was at the head of Job’s list because the eye is the first instrument of sin (Genesis 3:6). • To look with lust at a young woman violates the spirit of the seventh (Deuteronomy 5:18, see Matthew 5:27-28), and potentially the tenth (Deuteronomy 5:21), commandment.

Job called down curses on himself if he were guilty of the accusations made against him. Except for his mention of idolatry (Job 31:26-27), Job addressed his fidelity to God in terms of the second half of the Ten Commandments, summarized by the command to “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18; Romans 13:9).

If Job had lied to anyone as part of a business deal, it would violate the eighth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:19); if it occurred in court, it would violate the ninth (Deuteronomy 5:20). This sin would merit fiery judgment (Revelation 21:8). • If Job lusted for what his eyes had seen, he would violate the tenth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:21). • then let someone else eat: This was a self-curse.

Whether she seduced him or he waited for her (Job 24:15-16), if Job lusted for his neighbor’s wife he would break the seventh (Deuteronomy 5:18, Matthew 5:27-28) and tenth (Deuteronomy 5:21) commandments. • serve: Literally grind for. This might refer to servitude (Exodus 11:5) or to sexual intercourse.

The Hebrew term zimmah (shameful sin) is associated with sexual crimes such as incest (“wicked act,” Leviticus 18:17), gang-rape (“terrible . . . crime,” Judges 20:6), and prostitution (Ezekiel 23:49).
The association of fire with hell or the grave is rare in the Old Testament (cp. Deuteronomy 32:22).

unfair to . . . servants: This might refer to violations of the fourth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:12-15). • God created both me and my servants: Job extended the implications of being created in God’s image to the poor (Proverbs 14:31; Proverbs 22:2) and even to slaves.
knowing the judges would take my side: Job was respected and regarded as a member of the elite class (Job 29:7-10).
If an arm was used in sinful action (Job 31:21), having it torn from its socket would be a fitting punishment and better than facing God’s judgment (cp. Matthew 5:28-30).

Have I put my trust in . . . my gold: Job left the consequence of this oath unstated because the if-then pattern was now established (Job 31:5-23). He rejected Eliphaz’s implied judgment (Job 22:24-25; see Psalm 52:7; Psalm 62:10; 1 Tim 6:10, 17).
gloated about my wealth: See Deuteronomy 8:17-18; cp. Isaiah 10:12-14; Daniel 4:28-30; Hosea 12:8.

Have I looked at the sun . . . or the moon: This oath denies violation (cp. Jeremiah 8:2; Jeremiah 44:17; Ezekiel 8:16; Acts 7:43) of the first commandment (Deuteronomy 5:7; see Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:2-7).
Like adultery (cp. Job 31:1, Job 31:9-12), worshiping the sun and moon was a capital crime. Both were sins of the eye that enticed the heart, and both types of sin were tried before judges.
secretly enticed in my heart: See Job 31:9. • throw kisses at them in worship: Cp. 1 Kgs 19:18; Hosea 13:2.
In Israel, the judges (see Job 31:11) were to punish idol worship by execution (Deuteronomy 17:2-7). • Denying the God of heaven violated the first commandment (Deuteronomy 5:7).

rejoiced when disaster struck my enemies: See Proverbs 24:17-18; cp. 2 Sam 16:5-8. • Cursing anyone violated the spirit of the sixth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:17; see Matthew 5:21-22). • It was against God’s will to ask for revenge (Matthew 5:43-44; Romans 12:14; James 3:6-10; 1 Pet 3:9).

never turned away a stranger: The Old Testament values hospitality (Genesis 18:1-13; Genesis 19:2-3; Judges 19:20-21), and the New Testament commands it (Matthew 25:35; Romans 12:13; 1 Tim 3:2; Hebrews 13:2; 1 Pet 4:9).
sign my name: Job wanted to make the proceedings official (Job 19:23-24).
face the accusation proudly (literally carry it on my shoulder; cp. Exodus 28:12; Isaiah 22:22): He would take full responsibility for his actions.
A prince who had been wrongly accused had the right to come before his king to make an appeal.
The land was the chief witness to crimes committed upon it (Job 20:27; see Genesis 4:10; cp. James 5:4).
let thistles grow: Job’s curse on himself echoed God’s primal curse on Adam (Genesis 3:17-18; cp. Isaiah 7:25; Zephaniah 2:9).
Job’s three friends (see Job 2:11) failed to comfort him (Job 6:14-30; Job 13:4; Job 16:2; Job 19:21; Job 42:10).

Having completed three cycles of speeches between Job and his three friends, we now hear from a new voice. Elihu has not been previously introduced, but he is a young man who has listened to everything the others have said.

the Buzite: Buz had connections with Aram (Genesis 22:21) and Arabia (Jeremiah 25:23), as did Uz (Job 1:1). • Elihu repeatedly stated that he was angry; he probably regarded his anger as righteous zeal (Psalm 69:9).
Elihu’s deference to elders followed a well-known principle (see also Job 12:12; Job 15:10; Leviticus 19:32; 1 Tim 5:1; 1 Pet 5:5).

The spirit within people might not be the prophetic Spirit that Elihu later appeals to (Job 33:14-15), as Eliphaz had done (Job 4:12-17; cp. Job 32:18-20). This spirit might simply exist by virtue of creation (Job 33:4; Genesis 2:7; Acts 17:25).

As translated, the phrase you sit there . . . you are silent is addressed to Job’s friends. An alternate translation is they sit there . . . they are silent, in which case Elihu is speaking to Job about his friends.

The length of Elihu’s speech (Job 32:1–37:24) demonstrates that he truly was full of pent-up words. • Elihu probably thought the spirit (Hebrew ruakh) within him was prophetic urgency (Job 32:8, Job 32:19-20; Psalm 39:3), but the reader might find him full of wind (Hebrew ruakh; see study note on Job 15:2-3). • Like Zophar, Elihu must speak to find relief (cp. Job 20:2).
Listen: Elihu begged to be heard (Job 33:1; Job 34:2, Job 34:16), which is what Job had also sought (Job 13:6).
By inviting Job to make his case, Elihu acted as though he were God, or at least the arbiter that Job had been seeking (Job 9:32-35).

you don’t need to be afraid of me (literally my terror shall not make you afraid): God’s terrors (Job 6:4; Job 7:14; Job 9:34; Job 13:21; Job 23:15) had been thrown in Job’s face by Eliphaz (Job 15:21, Job 15:24; Job 22:10), Bildad (Job 18:11, Job 18:14), and Zophar (Job 20:25). • Elihu promised not to come down hard on Job, but later he broke his word (Job 34:7-9, Job 34:33-37).
You said: Job claimed to be pure and without sin, using various terms (Job 9:21; Job 10:6-7; Job 11:4; Job 13:23-24; Job 15:14-16; Job 16:17; Job 31:1-40).
Job frequently complained about God’s surveillance (Job 7:20; Job 10:14; Job 13:27); he wanted relief from having his every move scrutinized (Job 14:16; Job 29:2).
Job’s central complaint was that God does not respond (Job 9:16; Job 19:7; Job 23:2-7).
He speaks in dreams: See, e.g., Genesis 15:12; Genesis 20:3; Genesis 31:24; Genesis 40:1–41:36; Daniel 2:1-45; Joel 2:28; Acts 16:9-10.
from crossing over the river of death: This phrase may also be translated from passing [i.e., dying] by the sword. Both translations fit the context (cp. Job 36:12).
angels of death wait for them: Cp. Exodus 12:23; 2 Sam 24:16; 1 Cor 10:10.
An angel from heaven would intercede, taking the role of the mediator Job longed for (see Job 5:1; Job 9:33-34; Job 16:18-21).
The ransom is ultimately found in Christ (Matthew 20:28; Romans 3:24-25; 1 Tim 2:6; 1 Pet 1:18-19).
God will receive him with joy: Cp. Numbers 6:24-26; Psalm 67:1; Acts 2:28; Jude 1:24.
For Elihu to say that he was anxious to see Job justified sounds ironic; he had entered the discussion in the first place “because Job refused to admit that he had sinned” (Job 32:1-5).
ear tests . . . mouth distinguishes: Elihu echoed Job’s earlier complaint about the other counselors’ weak argument that “wisdom belongs to the aged” (Job 12:11-12; see Job 6:30; Hebrews 5:14).
Job had claimed to be innocent: See Job 9:20-21; Job 13:18; Job 27:6.

Eliphaz had accused Job of being a liar (Job 15:5), fulfilling Job’s earlier worry (Job 6:28-29). • My suffering (literally My arrow): For the link with the Lord’s arrows, see Job 6:4; Job 16:13; Jeremiah 10:19; Jeremiah 15:18; Jeremiah 30:12, Jeremiah 30:15; Lamentations 3:12; Micah 1:9; Nahum 3:19.

Elihu later repeated this accusation (Job 35:3; cp. Psalm 73:13; Zephaniah 1:12; Malachi 3:14), but he misrepresented Job’s words (Job 9:22-23; Job 21:15). Job had actually condemned those who held this view (Job 21:14-16).

The passage attaches three ideas to the truth that God can do no wrong (Job 34:10, Job 34:12): (1) God pays back all people according to their behavior (Job 34:11); (2) as the Creator, God is not answerable to anyone (Job 34:13); and (3) every living being depends upon God for its existence, and God can withdraw that gift without doing anything wrong (Job 34:14-15; cp. Romans 9:19-29).

according to their deeds: Cp. Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Jeremiah 32:19; Ezekiel 33:20; Matthew 16:27; Romans 2:6; Galatians 6:7-8; 1 Pet 1:17. The ultimate harvest will take place at the end of time (2 Cor 5:10; Revelation 2:23; Revelation 22:12).

The implied answer was that God could not govern if he hated justice (cp. Romans 3:4-7; Romans 7:7, Romans 7:13; Romans 9:14; Galatians 2:17; Galatians 6:14). • Later, God also asked if Job was going to condemn the almighty judge (Job 40:8).
doesn’t care how great a person may be: Impartiality flows from God’s justice (Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11; Galatians 2:6; Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 3:25; 1 Pet 1:17).
The wicked might try to hide in darkness (Jeremiah 23:24), but they will fail (Psalm 139:11-12; cp. Amos 9:2-3). God brings everything to light (1 Cor 4:5).
We don’t set the time: Elihu rejected Job’s wish for a quick (Job 21:19), published time of judgment (Job 24:1).
God knows everything without asking anyone (Job 34:25). • sets up others in their place: Daniel 2:21; Daniel 5:28-30.
When God renders justice openly, it leads to proper fear among the wicked (Deuteronomy 21:21; 1 Tim 5:20) and to public rejoicing among the righteous (cp. Exodus 14:30-31).
Why don’t people say? Elihu was indirectly asking, “Job, why won’t you admit it?”
deserve the maximum penalty: Zophar had also said that Job was being punished less than he deserved (Job 11:6).

Elihu attempted to answer his own question (Job 35:2), but his answer did not add to what Zophar (Job 11:8-9), Eliphaz (Job 22:12), Bildad (Job 25:5-6), and Job (Job 9:8-10) had already said. Elihu failed to recognize that all sin wrongs God (Genesis 39:9; Matthew 25:41-46; cp. Proverbs 19:17).
Elihu echoed and then rejected Job’s words (Job 9:24; Job 12:6-10; Job 21:7-15, Job 21:17).
Elihu echoed his earlier accusation (Job 34:35); later, God would agree (Job 38:2).
I am a man of great knowledge (literally one who is perfect in knowledge is with you): Elihu was probably claiming to be completely sincere or saying that his logic was flawless.
The biblical principle that God never takes his eyes off the innocent (2 Chr 16:9; Psalm 33:18; Psalm 34:15; 1 Pet 3:12) answered Job’s frustration about divine surveillance (Job 7:17-21).
If they listen and obey God, they will be blessed: This is a valid biblical principle of repentance (see Job 11:13-19; Job 22:21-25; Deuteronomy 4:30; Jeremiah 7:23; Jeremiah 26:13).
dying from lack of understanding: See also Job 4:21; Proverbs 5:23; Proverbs 10:21.

The Hebrew yadin can mean he governs or he nourishes, which parallels food in abundance (Job 38:26; Psalm 65:9-13; Psalm 104:13-15, Psalm 104:27-28). The more common meaning for yadin is “judge,” which would mean that God does all things to bless his people and judge his enemies (Job 37:11-13; Job 38:22-23; see Genesis 6:17; Genesis 19:24; Exodus 9:23-25; Joshua 10:11-14; 1 Sam 12:18).
The Old Testament often associates thunder with God’s voice (Job 36:29, Job 36:33; Job 37:5; Job 38:1; Exodus 19:16-19; Psalm 104:7).
everyone stops working . . . watch his power: The ending of the agricultural work season gave people time to meditate on God’s providential control.

The same act by God can serve more than one function, such as storms that both destroy enemies and give God’s people victory (Joshua 10:1-43; Judges 4:1-24; 1 Sam 7:10-11; Psalm 18:7-15; Psalm 105:32-33).
The hot south wind caused the sweltering conditions.
speak when they are confused? Or speak without being swallowed up? Punishment as severe as death might result from contesting God’s judgment (cp. Job 13:14).

the mountain of God (Hebrew from Zaphon): In the literature of the ancient city of Ugarit, Zaphon was the northern mountainous abode of Baal; here it figuratively refers to God’s lofty home in the heavens (see Isaiah 14:13-14).

cannot imagine the power of the Almighty: Cp. Job 11:7; Job 26:14; Romans 11:33; 1 Tim 6:16. • he is just and righteous: Cp. Job 9:4, Job 9:19; Job 12:13; Psalm 62:11; Psalm 66:3; Psalm 93:1; Psalm 99:4.

God challenged Job from out of the whirlwind. The Old Testament commonly associates storms with God’s presence (2 Kgs 2:1, 11; Ezekiel 1:4; Nahum 1:3). Job finally had an audience with God (Job 13:22-23).

God challenges Job, who acknowledges his inability to judge the moral world by demonstrating his ignorance of the natural world’s cosmic (Job 38:4-21) and meteorological elements (Job 38:22-38), animals, and birds (Job 38:39–39:30).
Finally, the Lord answered Job. In this final section, the Lord challenges Job’s overreaching self-defense with a display of his works that remind Job of God’s transcendent greatness.
questions my wisdom: God’s accusation sounds like a charge made by Eliphaz (Job 15:2) and Elihu (Job 34:35; Job 35:16) to which Job eventually admitted guilt (Job 42:3).
The morning stars are personified in parallel construction with the angels (Job 1:6; Job 2:1).
locked it behind barred gates: The sea is depicted as a dangerous creature kept under control.
it is robed in brilliant colors: The rising sun brings out the colors, shapes, and textures of things.
you were born before it was all created: Cp. Proverbs 8:25. This sarcasm resembles that of Eliphaz (Job 15:7).

Snow and hail are kept in divine storehouses such as those for the deep seas and winds (Psalm 33:7; Psalm 135:7; Jeremiah 10:13; Jeremiah 51:16). God uses these elements as weapons (Job 36:32; Isaiah 30:30; Ezekiel 13:11-13; Revelation 16:21) in the storms he sends on the day of battle and war (e.g., Joshua 10:11; Judges 5:20-21; 1 Sam 7:10).

The east wind blows off the desert to scorch crops (Genesis 41:6, Genesis 41:23, Genesis 41:27; Jeremiah 4:11; Jonah 4:8) and dry up seas (Exodus 14:21; Isaiah 11:15). It is an arid contrast to the torrents of rain that cause flooding. • Beneficial rain to satisfy the parched ground (Psalm 104:10-11; Psalm 107:35; Isaiah 35:7; Isaiah 58:11) stands in contrast to both scorching winds (Job 38:24) and flooding rains (Job 38:25).

heart . . . mind: These words can also be translated ibis . . . rooster. The Egyptians thought the ibis was wise about the flooding of the Nile, the most important seasonal event in Egypt; and Israel’s rabbis thought the rooster could forecast rain or that its crow distinguished day from night. The idea would then be Who taught the ibis and the rooster? See also Psalm 51:6; Proverbs 2:6; James 1:5, James 1:17.

wild donkey . . . hates (literally scorns) the noise of the city: This is the first in a series of animals that scorn others who are their inferiors in some way (cp. Job 39:18, Job 39:22; Job 41:29). These images illustrate how God scorns the opposition of a man like Job (see Psalm 2:4).

Now extinct and already rare by Moses’ time, the wild ox was the most powerful land animal in early Canaan. This Old Testament symbol of strength (Numbers 23:22; Numbers 24:8; Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 29:6; Psalm 92:10) was never tamed (cp. Genesis 1:28; Genesis 9:2; Psalm 8:5-6).
In the ancient Near East, the ostrich had a reputation as a bird that God had deprived of wisdom.

The ostrich is a symbol of neglect for her young (Lamentations 4:3) because she (1) lays her eggs on top of the earth; (2) appears to leave her eggs to die when a predator approaches them (although she is probably attempting to lure the predator away from the nest); and (3) lays her eggs with several other hens in one nest, so most of the eggs are not her own.
passes (literally scorns) the swiftest horse with its rider: See Job 39:7, Job 39:22; Job 41:29.
The ram’s horn was sounded in combat to call for the charge (Joshua 6:4-6).
Where there’s a carcass, there you’ll find it—feeding on the remains (Ezekiel 39:17-19; Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37).
