The Greek Old Testament omits this conclusion to God’s first speech.

Job’s brief and humble response does not acknowledge guilt, but it does admit his insignificance (Job 40:4). He had previously thought that he could approach God like a prince (Job 31:37) or even cross-examine him (Job 13:22-23).

I am nothing (cp. Job 42:6): Job was not repenting from sin; like Abraham, he recognized his unworthiness (Genesis 18:27). • Job had asked his comforters to cover their mouth to acknowledge shock (Job 21:5); here he does so himself in reaction to his own rash words.
Job had nothing more to say; he had no further charges against God, nor would he make a rebuttal.
The Lord repeated his earlier challenge (see Job 38:1-3).
Job’s words (Job 10:7; Job 27:2; Job 31:35-37) had angered Elihu (Job 32:2; Job 34:5); now God himself challenged them.
Job could not do God’s work of humbling the proud (Isaiah 2:11-12, Isaiah 2:17; James 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5-6) apart from God’s authority (Malachi 4:3; Romans 16:20).

Following a list of natural animals (Job 39:1-30), God described Behemoth (Job 40:15-24) and Leviathan (Job 41:1-34) as creatures that man cannot tame. Job couldn’t tame the wild donkey or ox (Job 39:5-12), let alone Behemoth and Leviathan (Job 40:15-24), but God created them and could control them, and Job had to acknowledge it (Job 41:2). • Here Behemoth seems to be a natural creature: (1) It is an animal that God made, just as he made Job (Job 40:15); (2) it is not a dreadful predator but eats grass like an ox (Job 40:15); and (3) it is in a poem describing God’s creation of the natural order, rather than in a mythological story of the world’s formation. Most commentators identify Behemoth with the hippopotamus, a huge, grass-eating animal (Job 40:15-19) that lies in the river among the lotus plants and reeds (Job 40:21). Like the wild ox, Behemoth is powerful (Job 40:16-18, Job 40:24; Job 39:11), yet is essentially peaceful (Job 40:20-23).

Unlike the peaceful Behemoth (Job 40:15-24), Leviathan was menacing (see also Job 3:8; Psalm 74:14; Psalm 104:26; Isaiah 27:1). Most commentators identify Leviathan with the crocodile, with its terrible jaws (Job 41:14) and armored hide (Job 41:15-17, Job 41:23), thrashing the water (Job 41:31-32). But Leviathan is a fire-breathing dragon (Job 41:18-21) that wraps its coils around the sun to cause an eclipse (Job 3:8-9). The background for Leviathan is the seven-headed sea monster that represents chaos in ancient Near Eastern mythology. In the biblical record, this unruly maritime monster is a frequent biblical image for chaos and wickedness, whose head the Lord crushes (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1; cp. Job 9:13; Job 26:12; Psalm 89:9-10; Isaiah 30:7; Isaiah 51:9). Later in the Bible, Satan is linked to the ancient serpent (Genesis 3:1-24) and unruly dragon (Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2), whose head Christ and his followers crush (Romans 16:20).

Job understood the message of God’s speeches: I know that you can do anything. Nothing is too hard for God (Genesis 18:14; Jeremiah 32:17; Matthew 19:26) and nothing can stop his plan (Job 23:13; Isaiah 14:27; Isaiah 46:10). Job realized how unlike God he was.
now I have seen you: Up to this point, Job had not seen God (see Job 23:8); now, like Isaiah, he had been in God’s presence and was overwhelmed by God’s holiness (Isaiah 6:1).

Eliphaz the Temanite was the spokesman for the friends, which probably indicates his seniority. Eliphaz had falsely implied that his advice originated in prophetic visions (Job 4:12-16); now God did speak to him, but not to affirm his message. • Unlike his three friends (cp. Job 13:7-10), Job had spoken accurately about God. Job’s blunt questions were better suited to arriving at the truth about God than the friends’ superficial orthodox doctrine.

The Lord made Job the mediator that Job had hoped to find for himself (Job 9:33; Job 16:19-21; Job 19:25) and that Elihu desired to be (Job 32:1–37:24). • go to my servant Job: God wanted Job’s friends to be reconciled with Job before they presented their offerings (Matthew 5:23-24). • My servant Job will pray for you; he had also prayed for his children (Job 1:5; cp. James 5:16; 1 Jn 5:16). • When the Lord accepted Job’s prayer, it ironically fulfilled Eliphaz’s promise (Job 22:26-30).
Job’s fortunes probably included his health (Job 42:16-17). God created humans in order to bless them, not curse them.

Although Job was restored, he still needed to be consoled and comforted for the loss of his children. Following Job’s own earlier practice (Job 4:4; Job 16:5), his family and former friends took up where the three other friends left off (Job 2:11; cp. 2 Cor 7:6). • The gift of money was not so much charity to provide a financial basis for Job’s restored fortune as it was to honor and seek the favor of an influential man (e.g., Proverbs 18:16), and perhaps even to assuage disfavor (e.g., Genesis 32:20; Genesis 33:10; Genesis 43:11; 1 Sam 25:27). • A gold ring was worn in a woman’s nose (Genesis 24:47; Proverbs 11:22; Isaiah 3:21) or on the ears of either men or women (Genesis 35:4; Exodus 32:2-3; Judges 8:24).
When God blessed Job, it ironically fulfilled Bildad’s promise (Job 8:7).

The beautiful names of Job’s new daughters spoke of Job’s renewed and pleasant good fortunes. • Jemimah means “dove” (see Song of Solomon 2:14). • Keziah means “cassia” or “cinnamon flower” (see Psalm 45:8). • Keren-happuch means “horn of antimony,” which refers to a lustrous container for cosmetics.

their father put them into his will: Daughters normally inherited only when there were no male heirs (Numbers 27:1-23; Numbers 36:1-13). Perhaps Job’s unusual action expressed his superabundant prosperity; only a wealthy man could afford to pass some of his wealth to the families into which his daughters would marry.

140 years was twice the normal life span (Psalm 90:10). If the analogy of double restoration holds (Job 42:10), Job might have been 70 already and then lived another 140 years. A life span of 210 years would not be out of keeping with the patriarchal setting of the book (see Genesis 25:7; Genesis 35:28; Genesis 47:28; Genesis 50:26; Deuteronomy 34:7; Joshua 24:29). • living to see four generations of his children and grandchildren: Job’s blessing extended to watching his multigenerational family grow (Genesis 50:23; Psalm 128:6).

Like Abraham and Isaac, who also died at a ripe old age (Genesis 25:8; Genesis 35:29), Job lived a long, full life, fulfilling Eliphaz’s promise (Job 5:26), which was based on God’s general promise (Deuteronomy 6:2; Psalm 91:16). • At the end of the book, the Greek Old Testament adds a note declaring that Job will rise from the dead at the resurrection. It goes on to provide information about where and when Job and his descendants lived.
